explanations.positive_explanation: This feature lights up on “boilerplate” or system-level instruction text—things like forum/posting rules, cookie-consent prompts, Apache license headers, etc. It particularly picks out the functional words and verbs (post, continue, obtain, or, at, etc.) in those formal, normative statements rather than ordinary prose.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on the words that serve as high‐level headings, titles, captions or bylines—the structural labels that kick off new sections or mark metadata (e.g. article titles, “By …” lines, section headers, image captions, notices, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the very start of a new document or section header—anything that looks like a title or metadata block (e.g. comment‐style license headers, “Abstract:” or paper titles, Q/A titles, numbered lists, section labels, etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees a “block‐ender” token—a period or line‐break marking the end of a sentence, title, heading or list item.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on abstract nominalizations—nouns (often ending in ‑ion/-ment/-ence/-t) that denote intangible concepts or evaluations (e.g. “effects,” “disconnect,” “delight,” “advent,” “role,” “frustration,” “importance,” “relevance,” “dismay,” “problem,” “resentment”) used to structure or qualify discourse.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on the “banner” or header region at the top of a text or source file—i.e. the formal metadata block (copyright/licensing notices, legal‐opinion headings, module/package/import declarations, ASCII border lines, etc.) that kicks off a document.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on the little “pivot” words that introduce or link to a sentence’s main proposition or emphasis—above all the copular verbs (is, was, be) plus a handful of discourse-marker/intensifier tokens (literally, now, disposition, reported below, etc.) that similarly flag the core assertion or call-to-action in a clause.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature picks up on the double‐asterisk (“**”) markers used to denote bolded or strongly emphasized headings/titles (i.e. the closing ** delimiters in markdown-style formatting) across a variety of web-sourced text.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron lights up on the “file‐prologue” boilerplate you see at the very top of source files—import/using/module declarations, DOCTYPE or HTML/XML prologs, license/header comments and assembly/type metadata that kick off a file.
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on the token that closes off a headline or sentence—typically the final word or punctuation (e.g. a period, question mark, or end-of-headline word) marking the boundary of a news title or article snippet.

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires whenever we hit a relational preposition—“of,” “with,” “by,” “to,” etc.—that kicks off a prepositional phrase linking two entities (possession, agency, accompaniment, direction, and so on). In effect it is a PP-phrase boundary detector marking those little function-word introductions.
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on the “**” emphasis markers (and the first/last words they surround), i.e. it flags bold-formatted section titles and headlines across different document types.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature detects the structural markers of section headings in scientific/technical documents—titles like “Introduction,” “Background,” “Findings,” the accompanying underlines or equals signs, and the section‐ID tags (e.g. “{#Sec1}”).
explanations.negative_explanation: This neuron fires on tokens that kick off a new “block” or heading—i.e. the markers and first words of section titles, document headers or metadata lines (bold/asterisk wrappers, patent “Field of the Invention,” news datelines, code‐factory declarations, citation lines, etc.).

explanations.positive_explanation: This neuron fires on the kind of fixed, highly formulaic “front‐matter” you see at the top of files and legal briefs—those boilerplate header blocks that announce the document’s identity or authority (e.g. court-case captions like “IN THE COURT OF APPEALS,” license preambles like “Licensed under the Apache License,” etc.).
explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that are part of high‐level document or section headers and metadata—e.g. case‐caption lines in legal opinions, article or chapter titles and bylines, license‐block headers in code, and other all‐caps/separator‐rich headings that mark the start of a new section.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature is a “section‐heading/title” detector – it lights up on the big, often all-caps or specially marked tokens that introduce a new section or document (e.g. “Main menu,” “News,” post titles, article headings, product/service names or code‐comment banners).

explanations.negative_explanation: This feature fires on subword tokens that serve as formal “resource identifiers” in technical text—things like domain suffixes (​.com​), filesystem segments (​/usr​, ​share​), package/import paths (​github​.com, ​golang​.org), file-name components (​cancer​ in TIFFs), legal-document codes (ORN in CALIFORNIA), and similar structured names or namespaces. It effectively flags the bits of text that identify external resources or named entities in code and documentation.

explanations.positive_explanation: This feature fires on tokens that serve as high-level document or page headings—i.e. the first, often capitalized or numeric words of titles, section labels, navigation/menu items and other structural headers across blogs, docs and web pages.
explanations.negative_explanation: This head is a detector for fragments of systematic chemical names (especially organic‐chemistry morphemes like “amino,” “–ol,” “phen,” “nitro/ros,” “hydro,” numeric locants, etc.), i.e. subword pieces typical of technical compound nomenclature.
